pos: n. (Jean Crespin, c. 1520–1572, Genevan printer and martyrologist of the French church)
etymology: French Jean, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Crespin, from Latin crispus, curly-haired.
biblical_def: Jean Crespin was a lawyer of Arras who fled to Geneva in 1548, set up as a printer, and over the next twenty years produced both a great deal of Calvin and the book that preserved the French Reformation's memory of its own dead. His Book of Martyrs, first issued in 1554 and enlarged through edition after edition until his death in the plague of 1572, collects the examinations, letters and last words of men and women executed for the gospel in France, the Low Countries, England, Spain and Italy. Crespin's method is the printer's: wherever he can get the actual document — the record of the trial, the letter smuggled from the cell — he prints it and stands aside. The result is a book in which the martyrs speak in their own voices and the hostile court speaks in its own, and the reader is left to weigh the exchange. It is the model Foxe worked from. “And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held” (Rev 6:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines martyrology as a history or account of martyrs, and register as a written account or entry of acts and proceedings.
webster_full: MARTYROL'OGY, n. A history or account of martyrs with their sufferings; a register of martyrs.
REG'ISTER, n. A written account or entry of acts, judgments or proceedings.
EXAMINA'TION, n. In judicial proceedings, a careful inquiry into facts by testimony.
PRINT'ER, n. One that prints books, pamphlets or papers.
scriptures: Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.
corruption_summary: The Genevan printer who collected the examinations and letters of the French martyrs.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the dismissal of all martyrology as hagiography, a genre whose conventions guarantee that every sufferer is serene and every judge is a monster. The charge has force against some of the literature and very little against Crespin, whose practice was to print the documents. Where he has the trial record he gives it, and the judges in his pages argue competently and the martyrs sometimes falter.

The principle to recover is that Scripture itself keeps a register of this kind and places it in the most solemn setting available. “I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held” (Rev 6:9). They are counted, and the ground of their death is specified twice. John adds what overcame the accuser, and it is a document before it is anything else: “the word of their testimony” (Rev 12:11).

pos: n. (Adriaan van Haemstede, c. 1525–1562, Dutch martyrologist and preacher of Antwerp)
etymology: Latin Hadrianus, of the Adriatic; Dutch van Haemstede, of Haamstede, a village of Zeeland.
biblical_def: Adriaan van Haemstede was the first preacher of the Reformed congregation at Antwerp, working underground in a city under Spanish rule, and in 1559 he published the first Dutch martyrology, a history of the men and women killed for the faith from the apostles to his own year. He wrote it in the middle of the danger he was describing. His later career was unhappy: driven from Antwerp, he went to the Dutch congregation in London, where he insisted that the Anabaptists in the city, though in grave error on the person of Christ, were brethren who should be dealt with rather than denounced. The congregation excommunicated him and he died in Friesland in his thirties under that sentence. His judgment about the Anabaptists was wrong, because a man who denies that Christ took flesh of the Virgin denies the gospel; his instinct to pursue the error patiently rather than hand men over was not. The book he left outlived the quarrel. “And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony” (Rev 12:11).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines excommunicate as to expel from communion with a church, and chronicle as a historical account of facts in order of time.
webster_full: EXCOMMU'NICATE, v. To expel from communion; to eject from the communion of the church by an ecclesiastical sentence.
CHRON'ICLE, n. An historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time.
CLANDES'TINE, a. Secret; private; hidden; withdrawn from public view.
SCHIS'MATIC, n. One who separates from an established church on account of a diversity of opinions.
scriptures: And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
Hereby know ye the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God:

And every spirit that confesseth not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is not of God: and this is that spirit of antichrist, whereof ye have heard that it should come; and even now already is it in the world.
In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves; if God peradventure will give them repentance to the acknowledging of the truth;
corruption_summary: The first Dutch martyrology, written underground, and an excommunication its author died under.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is in the position Haemstede took in London, and it must be named even while his motive is honoured. He wanted to treat the Antwerp Anabaptists as erring brethren. But the error in question was not a secondary one: those he defended denied that Christ took real flesh from Mary, and John supplies the test by which that denial is measured and finds it to be the spirit of antichrist.

The principle to recover is that the test of a teacher is Christological and that John states it without any room for degree. “Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God” (1Jo 4:2), and the converse is given in the next verse in the same words. That settles who is a brother. It does not settle the manner, and Paul's charge still binds over the top of it: “In meekness instructing those that oppose themselves” (2Ti 2:25). Haemstede had the second half and lost the first.

pos: n. (Ludwig Rabus, 1524–1592, Lutheran martyrologist of Strasbourg and Ulm)
etymology: German Ludwig, famous in war; Rabus, a latinised form of Rab, a raven.
biblical_def: Ludwig Rabus was a Strasbourg preacher who between 1552 and 1558 brought out eight volumes of Histories of the Holy Chosen Witnesses, Confessors and Martyrs — the first great Protestant martyrology, published before Crespin's was enlarged and before Foxe's existed, and the source both of them drew on. He runs the line from the prophets and apostles through the early church and the medieval dissenters to his own century, and the structure is itself the argument: the true church is the suffering one, identifiable in every age by what is done to it rather than by its buildings or its succession. Rabus was a hard Lutheran who afterwards, as superintendent at Ulm, made himself unpleasant to everyone not of his own party, and he quarrelled bitterly with Katharina Schütz Zell in Strasbourg over her hospitality to the heterodox. The eight volumes remain the foundation of the genre. “They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword” (Heb 11:37).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines witness as one who gives testimony, and succession as a series of persons following one another in an office.
webster_full: WIT'NESS, n. Testimony; attestation of a fact or event; that which furnishes evidence or proof.
SUCCES'SION, n. A series of persons or things following one another in order of time.
CON'FESSOR, n. One who makes a profession of his faith in the Christian religion, and adheres to it in spite of persecution.
PERSECU'TION, n. The act or practice of pursuing with enmity and malignity, particularly for adherence to a religious creed.
scriptures: They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, were tempted, were slain with the sword: they wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins; being destitute, afflicted, tormented;
(Of whom the world was not worthy:) they wandered in deserts, and in mountains, and in dens and caves of the earth.
Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.
Remember the word that I said unto you, The servant is not greater than his lord. If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they have kept my saying, they will keep yours also.
corruption_summary: Eight volumes of witnesses, the first Protestant martyrology and the source of the rest.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the inversion of Rabus's argument into a test: that suffering identifies the true church, therefore whoever suffers is the true church. That is not what Hebrews says and it is not what his own practice assumed, since he excluded from his volumes the Anabaptists who were dying in the same decade. Persecution is a mark of the true church, not a proof of any particular sufferer's doctrine.

The principle to recover is the one Paul states as a flat generalisation, with no qualification about era or country: “Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” (2Ti 3:12). The Lord grounds it in his own treatment and in the servant's relation to his master: “The servant is not greater than his lord. If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (Joh 15:20). Hebrews supplies the verdict the world is unqualified to give, in a parenthesis: “(Of whom the world was not worthy:)” (Heb 11:38).

pos: n. (John Bale, 1495–1563, English antiquary, bishop of Ossory and controversialist)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; English Bale, from Old English bealu, or from a place-name in Norfolk.
biblical_def: John Bale was a Carmelite friar who came over to the Reformation, married, wrote plays, and became the most abusive controversialist in England; his contemporaries called him bilious Bale and he did not dispute it. He is worth an entry for two things that have nothing to do with his temper. First, when the monastic libraries were being broken up he went round them listing and rescuing what he could, and his catalogues of British writers preserve the record of hundreds of manuscripts that were afterwards destroyed — one of the few men in England who saw what was being lost and tried to keep an account of it. Second, he was briefly bishop of Ossory in Ireland under Edward VI, where he insisted on the English ordinal against local resistance, and fled on Mary's accession after his servants were killed. He spent the Marian years at Basel with Foxe and shaped the historical framework of the Acts and Monuments. “Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines antiquary as one versed in antiquity, and catalogue as a list or enumeration of names or things in order.
webster_full: AN'TIQUARY, n. One versed in antiquity; a person who studies the monuments and remains of ancient times.
CAT'ALOGUE, n. A list or enumeration of the names of men or things disposed in a certain order.
DISSOLU'TION, n. The act of breaking up an assembly; the destruction of a body by the separation of its parts.
SCUR'RILOUS, a. Using the low and indecent language of the meaner sort of people; grossly opprobrious.
scriptures: Jer 6:16
Thus saith the LORD, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. But they said, We will not walk therein.
Psa 78:4
We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
Eph 4:29
Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.
And further, by these, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.
corruption_summary: The friar turned antiquary who catalogued the monastic libraries as they were destroyed.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name in Bale is his tongue, and his own side said so at the time. He was capable of real research and incapable of courtesy, and the abuse in his controversial writing did his cause measurable harm: it gave his opponents an easy answer and it hardened men who might have been persuaded. A true position argued foully is still a true position and is less likely to be heard.

The principle to recover is that Scripture regulates the manner of speech for the sake of the hearer and makes edification the test. “Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers” (Eph 4:29). Bale's better instinct was the antiquarian one, and that too is scriptural. Jeremiah's standing instruction is to go and look at what was there before: “ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein” (Jer 6:16).

pos: n. (John Ponet, c. 1514–1556, bishop of Winchester and author of a treatise on political power)
etymology: Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; English Ponet, from a Kentish surname.
biblical_def: John Ponet was a Cambridge scholar, chaplain to Cranmer, bishop of Rochester and then of Winchester under Edward VI, and a Marian exile at Strasbourg, where he died at forty-two. He wrote a catechism for the Edwardian church and, in 1556, a Short Treatise of Politic Power, which is one of the first works in English to argue that a ruler who governs against the law of God may lawfully be resisted, and in extremity removed, by the lesser magistrates and the estates of the realm. The book was written by a man whose brethren were being burned at home and it reads like it. It is the English root of the resistance theory that runs through Knox, the Huguenots and the Covenanters. The doctrine requires careful handling and the Reformed tradition has handled it carefully: resistance is by the lesser magistrate, in his office, not by the private subject arming himself, and the distinction between those two things is the whole difference between a vindication of law and a rebellion. “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tyranny as arbitrary or despotic exercise of power, and magistrate as a public civil officer invested with authority.
webster_full: TYR'ANNY, n. Arbitrary or despotic exercise of power; the exercise of power over subjects beyond what the laws permit.
MAG'ISTRATE, n. A public civil officer, invested with the executive government or some branch of it.
RESIST'ANCE, n. The act of resisting; opposition; the quality of not yielding to force.
ES'TATE, n. In a political sense, an order or class of men in the body politic.
scriptures: Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Dan 3:18
But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.
corruption_summary: The exiled bishop whose treatise is the English root of Reformed resistance theory.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse runs both ways and both are dangerous. One reads Ponet as a licence for private revolt, which he did not teach: his resistance is lodged in the lesser magistrate acting in his office and in the estates of the realm, which is a constitutional argument, not an invitation to the individual subject. The other dismisses the whole tradition as rebellion dressed up, which has to ignore the three Hebrews and the apostles before the Sanhedrin.

The principle to recover is that Scripture holds two things at once and the Reformed tradition has refused to drop either. Subjection is the rule and it is stated absolutely: “Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers” (Rom 13:1). Obedience to the magistrate stops where he commands sin, and there the answer is given without apology: “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). The three in Babylon show the temper of lawful refusal, with no sword and no plot: “we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image” (Dan 3:18).

pos: n. (Thomas Becon, c. 1512–1567, English devotional writer and chaplain to Cranmer)
etymology: Greek Thomas, from Aramaic teoma, a twin; English Becon, a variant of Beacon, a signal fire.
biblical_def: Thomas Becon was the most widely read English religious writer of the mid-sixteenth century and is now almost entirely forgotten. He wrote for households: a catechism cast as a father instructing his son, books of prayer for the sick and the dying, a manual for the newly married, treatises on fasting, on the sacraments, on the Lord's Prayer, and the Jewel of Joy, which contains a famous passage lamenting the enclosure of the common fields and the eviction of the poor from the land. He wrote in plain English for people who had a little education and a few shillings. He recanted under Henry VIII and lived in hiding in the midlands under another name, served as Cranmer's chaplain under Edward, was imprisoned and then exiled under Mary, and came home under Elizabeth. His collected works ran to three folio volumes in 1564. The devotional writer who supplies a nation's households with their prayers shapes more Christians than most theologians do. “And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart” (Deu 6:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines devotional as pertaining to devotion, and enclosure as the separating of common land by a fence.
webster_full: DEVO'TIONAL, a. Pertaining to devotion; used in devotion; as a devotional posture.
ENCLO'SURE, n. The act of enclosing; the separation of land from common grounds by a fence.
MAN'UAL, n. A small book, such as may be carried in the hand; a book of instruction.
HOUSE'HOLD, n. Those who dwell under the same roof and compose a family; domestic.
scriptures: Deu 6:6
And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart:
Col 3:16
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
Isa 5:8
Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place, that they may be placed alone in the midst of the earth!
Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
corruption_summary: The household writer who gave Tudor England its prayers, and denounced the enclosures.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern division between devotional writing and serious theology, which treats the first as a soft genre for private comfort. Becon's household books carry the doctrine of the Edwardian church in the form in which most English people actually received it, and the same pen that wrote prayers for the sick wrote a denunciation of the enclosing landlords that no bishop improved on.

The principle to recover is that the household is the unit Scripture addresses for the keeping of the word, and that nothing reaches a nation that has not reached its kitchens. “And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart” (Deu 6:6), and the teaching that follows is domestic in every clause. The prophetic word against the engrossing of land is equally plain: “Woe unto them that join house to house, that lay field to field, till there be no place” (Isa 5:8).

pos: n. (Alexander Nowell, c. 1517–1602, dean of St Paul's and author of the Elizabethan catechisms)
etymology: Greek Alexandros, defender of men; English Nowell, from Old French noel, the nativity.
biblical_def: Alexander Nowell was dean of St Paul's for forty years and the catechist of the Elizabethan church. A Marian exile at Frankfurt and Strasbourg, he came home at the accession and wrote three catechisms — a large, a middle and a small — of which the middle one was authorised by Convocation in 1563 and used in the grammar schools for a generation. They are thoroughly Reformed: election is taught plainly, the Supper is a spiritual feeding on Christ received by faith and not a bodily presence, and the ten commandments are expounded with the second standing on its own against images. The doctrinal position of the Elizabethan church is often argued about from the Articles alone; the catechisms show what was actually taught to children in English schools under the queen's authority, which is a better guide to what a church believes than its most carefully negotiated formulary. Nowell also preached before Elizabeth and was once stopped by her in the middle of a sermon for pressing too hard against images. “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines catechist as one who instructs by question and answer, and convocation as an assembly of the clergy for consultation.
webster_full: CAT'ECHIST, n. One who instructs by question and answer, particularly in the rudiments of the Christian religion.
CONVOCA'TION, n. An assembly of the clergy, by their representatives, to consult on ecclesiastical affairs.
DEAN, n. In England, an ecclesiastical dignitary in cathedral churches, the head of a chapter.
RU'DIMENT, n. A first principle or element; the first rules or principles of any art or science.
scriptures: Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
Eph 6:4
And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord.
And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.
Exo 20:4
Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:
corruption_summary: The dean whose catechisms show what the Elizabethan church actually taught its children.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the argument that the Church of England under Elizabeth was doctrinally indeterminate, a settlement of words permitting any reading. The catechisms answer it from the schoolroom. A child in an English grammar school in the 1570s was taught election, was taught that the bread remains bread and that Christ is received by faith, and was taught the second commandment against images, on the authority of Convocation.

The principle to recover is that catechising is a command with a promise and a method, and the method is relentless repetition in the ordinary course of a day. Solomon gives the promise: “Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it” (Pro 22:6). Paul gives the father the charge in one phrase: “bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord” (Eph 6:4), and names the result in Timothy's case: “from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures” (2Ti 3:15).

pos: n. (Edwin Sandys, c. 1519–1588, archbishop of York)
etymology: Old English Eadwine, rich friend; English Sandys, a variant of Sands, dweller by the sandy ground.
biblical_def: Edwin Sandys was vice-chancellor of Cambridge when the Duke of Northumberland came north in 1553, and he was made to preach the sermon supporting Lady Jane Grey's title. When Mary prevailed he was arrested for it, held in the Tower and the Marshalsea, and escaped abroad. He spent the Marian years at Strasbourg, Zurich and Frankfurt, came home at Elizabeth's accession, and was successively bishop of Worcester, bishop of London and archbishop of York. His sermons survive and they are plainly Reformed; he worked on the Bishops' Bible; he pressed against clerical vestments and lost that argument, conforming with open reluctance. He quarrelled, was the victim of a crude attempt at blackmail, and was by all accounts a difficult colleague. What he is useful for is the plain demonstration of where the Elizabethan episcopate stood. A man who had been an exile in Zurich, who disliked the vestments and said so, who preached election from a cathedral pulpit, became archbishop of York. “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines archbishop as a chief bishop who superintends the conduct of other bishops, and vestment as a garment worn in religious ceremonies.
webster_full: ARCHBISH'OP, n. A chief bishop; a church dignitary of the first class; a metropolitan bishop.
VEST'MENT, n. A garment; particularly, a long outer garment worn in religious ceremonies.
EX'ILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country.
CONFORM'ITY, n. Correspondence with a model or example; compliance with an established form.
scriptures: Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.
How shall we sing the LORD'S song in a strange land?
Rom 8:30
Moreover whom he did predestinate, them he also called: and whom he called, them he also justified: and whom he justified, them he also glorified.
Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.
corruption_summary: The Zurich exile who became archbishop of York, and conformed on the vestments under protest.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the tidy division of the Elizabethan church into Puritans who objected and bishops who did not. Sandys objected, lost, and conformed, saying publicly that he thought the garments indifferent in themselves and the imposition of them unwise. A great many of the early Elizabethan bishops were in that position, which is why the vestiarian quarrel was so bitter: it was not a fight between parties but a fight inside the same men.

The principle to recover is that conscience bound on a thing genuinely indifferent is a heavy burden, and that the apostolic instruction is to hold the substance fast while the circumstances are contested. “Hold fast the form of sound words” (2Ti 1:13). The doctrine Sandys preached from York is the chain Paul sets out in Romans: “whom he did predestinate, them he also called” (Rom 8:30). And over a long and quarrelsome public career stands the usual warning: “let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” (1Co 10:12).

pos: n. (James Pilkington, c. 1520–1576, bishop of Durham, the first Protestant to hold that see)
etymology: Hebrew Yaaqob, a supplanter, through Latin Jacobus; English Pilkington, from a Lancashire place-name.
biblical_def: James Pilkington was master of St John's College, Cambridge, an exile at Zurich, Basel and Geneva under Mary, and from 1561 the first Protestant bishop of Durham — the hardest diocese in England to reform, conservative, remote, and in 1569 the centre of the Northern Rising, during which the rebels restored the mass in Durham cathedral and Pilkington had to leave the county. He wrote commentaries on Haggai, Obadiah and Nehemiah, and they are the most interesting thing he left: all three are Old Testament books about rebuilding a ruined house of God in a hostile province, and he preached them to a diocese in precisely that condition. He founded the grammar school at Rivington in his native Lancashire, endowed it himself, and it survives. His sermons complain steadily about the poverty of the northern clergy and the pillaging of church revenues by gentlemen. “Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste” (Neh 2:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines see as the seat of episcopal power, a diocese, and rising as an insurrection, a tumultuous assembly.
webster_full: SEE, n. The seat of episcopal power; a diocese; the jurisdiction of a bishop.
RI'SING, n. The act of getting up; an insurrection; a tumultuous assembly.
COMMEN'TARY, n. A series of comments or annotations; an exposition of a book.
ENDOW', v. To enrich with a permanent fund or property; to settle a provision upon.
scriptures: Neh 2:17

Then said I unto them, Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste, and the gates thereof are burned with fire: come, and let us build up the wall of Jerusalem, that we be no more a reproach.
Neh 4:6
So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work.
Hag 1:4
Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?
Hag 2:4

Yet now be strong, O Zerubbabel, saith the LORD; and be strong, O Joshua, son of Josedech, the high priest; and be strong, all ye people of the land, saith the LORD, and work: for I am with you, saith the LORD of hosts:
corruption_summary: Durham's first Protestant bishop, preaching Haggai and Nehemiah to a province in ruins.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is a reading of the Northern Rising of 1569 as a popular revolt against an alien religion imposed from London, which is how it is often presented and which contains just enough truth to mislead. The north was conservative and the imposition was real. The rising was also led by two earls with dynastic ambitions, it restored the mass by force of arms, and it was crushed with several hundred hangings that did the Protestant cause in the north no good at all.

The principle to recover is the one Pilkington chose to preach, which is that rebuilding is slow, resisted, and commanded anyway. Nehemiah states the condition honestly before he states the task: “Ye see the distress that we are in, how Jerusalem lieth waste” (Neh 2:17). Haggai rebukes the inverted priorities that leave the house waste: “Is it time for you, O ye, to dwell in your cieled houses, and this house lie waste?” (Hag 1:4). And then the encouragement with its reason attached: “be strong, all ye people of the land, saith the LORD, and work: for I am with you” (Hag 2:4).

pos: n. (Richard Cox, c. 1500–1581, bishop of Ely and leader of the prayer-book party at Frankfurt)
etymology: Germanic Richard, strong in rule; English Cox, from cock, a byname, with the genitive ending.
biblical_def: Richard Cox was tutor to Edward VI, dean of Christ Church, chancellor of Oxford, and under Elizabeth bishop of Ely for twenty-two years. He is remembered chiefly for the quarrel at Frankfurt in 1555, where the English exiles divided over worship: Knox and the party with him wanted a simpler order on the Genevan model, Cox and his party insisted on the second Edwardian prayer book entire, and Cox won by manoeuvre — the newly arrived Coxians bought the citizenship of the town, gained the vote, and then had Knox removed from the city by reporting his earlier writing against the emperor to the magistrates. It was a shabby business and it set the English church's course. Cox was afterwards a competent and Reformed bishop who resisted the queen's raids on episcopal lands and refused to let a crucifix stand in her chapel. The troubles at Frankfurt are the seed of a hundred years of English division, and they turned on a procedural trick. “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines liturgy as a formulary of public devotions, and faction as a party combined for a particular purpose.
webster_full: LIT'URGY, n. A formulary of public devotions; the established formulas of public worship.
FAC'TION, n. A party, in political society, combined or acting in union, in opposition to the prince or state.
EX'ILE, n. Banishment; the person banished.
MANEU'VER, n. Management with address or artful design; stratagem.
scriptures: Let all things be done decently and in order.

Now I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that ye all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you; but that ye be perfectly joined together in the same mind and in the same judgment.
Php 2:3
Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
Jam 3:16
For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work.
corruption_summary: The Frankfurt quarrel of 1555, won by a trick, and a hundred years of English division after it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the retrospective reading of the Frankfurt troubles as the honest first encounter of two legitimate traditions, each holding a principled view of worship. The principles were real. The means by which the dispute was settled were not principled at all: a party bought the town's citizenship to gain votes and then used a civil denunciation to get the other side's leader expelled.

The principle to recover is that the manner of a church's disputing is itself under judgment, and James states the consequence as a simple rule of cause and effect. “For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work” (Jam 3:16). Confusion is exactly what Frankfurt produced and bequeathed. Paul's requirement is not merely that the right side win but that the contending be done in a particular temper: “Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory” (Php 2:3).

usage: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — Frankfurt, 1555.
“where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work” (Jam 3:16) — Knox expelled by denunciation.
“Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory” (Php 2:3) — the seed of a century of division.
